text:
But now take the doctor, as I tell you. Heed a friend’s advice; that prince is, after all, a half-old fool. — And in my agitation I lied about him, exaggerated his age, said that he was bald, that he was almost completely blind; I also claimed that he wore that crown on his shirt buttons solely and entirely to flaunt his nobility. — Besides, I have not bothered to get to know him, I said. There is nothing in him that marks him out in any way, he lacks the main lines, he is nothing.

But he is something, he is something! she screamed, and her voice cracked with anger. He is much more than you think, you forest creature! But just you wait, oh, he will speak to you, I shall ask him to. You do not believe that I love him, but you shall see that you are wrong. I will marry him, I shall think of him night and day. Remember that I say: I love him. Just let Eva come, ha-ha, God in heaven, just let her come, it is so unspeakably indifferent to me. Yes, I must see about getting away from here +++. She began to walk down the path from the hut, she took a few small, eager steps, turned around, still deathly pale in the face, and groaned: And never come before my eyes again.

XXV

The leaves are turning yellow, the potato tops had grown tall and were in bloom, hunting season came again, I shot ptarmigan, black grouse, and hares; one day I shot an eagle. Still, high sky, cool nights, many clear notes and piercing sounds in forest and field. Great and peaceful, the world rested ....

I have heard nothing further from Mr. Mack concerning the two auks I shot, I said to the doctor.

You may thank Edvarda for that, he replied. I know it; I heard that she opposed it.

I do not thank her, I said ....

Indian summer, Indian summer. The paths lay like belts through the yellowing forest, a new star appeared each day, the moon could be glimpsed like a shadow, a shadow of gold dipped in silver ....

God help you, you are married, Eva?

Did you not know?

No, I did not know.

Silently, she clasped my hand.

God help you, child, what are we to do now?

Whatever you wish. Perhaps you are not leaving yet; I will be happy as long as you are here.

No, Eva.

Yes, yes, only as long as you are here!

She looks forsaken and keeps clasping my hand.

No, Eva, go! Never again!

And nights pass and days come. It is already the third day since this conversation. Eva walks along the road carrying a load. How much firewood this child has carried home from the forest this summer! Put down your load, Eva, and let me see whether your eyes are still as blue.

Her eyes were red.

No, smile again, Eva! I resist you no longer, I am yours, I am yours ....

Evening. Eva sings; I hear her song, and a heat passes through me.

You are singing tonight, Eva?

Yes, I am happy.

And because she is shorter than I am, she jumps up a little to put her arms around my neck.

But Eva, you have torn your hands? Dear God, if only you had not torn them!

It does not matter.

Her face shines so wondrously.

Eva, have you spoken with Mr. Mack?

Once.

What did he say, and what did you say?

He has become very harsh toward us; he makes my husband work night and day on the wharf, and he sets me to all kinds of work as well. He has ordered me to do men’s work.

Why does he do that?

Eva looks down.

Why does he do that, Eva?

Because I love you.

But how can he know that?

I have told him.

Pause.

God grant that he were not so harsh toward you, Eva!

But it does not matter. Nothing matters now.

And her voice sounded in the forest exactly like a little trembling song.

And the leaves turn yellower still, it is drawing toward autumn, a few more stars have appeared in the sky, and from now on the moon looks like a shadow of silver dipped in gold. There was no cold, nothing, only a cool stillness and a streaming life in the forest. Every tree stood thinking. The berries were ripe.

Then came the twenty-second of August and the three iron nights.

XXVI

The first iron night.

At nine o’clock the sun goes down. A dim darkness settles over the earth, a couple of stars can be seen; two hours later, a gleam of the moon can be seen. I wander into the forest with my gun and my dog, I make a fire, and the light from my fire shines in among the pine trunks. There is no frost.

The first iron night, I say. And a bewilderingly intense joy at the time and the place strangely shakes me through and through ....

A toast, you human beings and animals and birds, to the solitary night in forests, in forests! A toast to the darkness and God’s murmuring among the trees, to the sweet, simple harmony of silence against my ears, to green leaves and yellow leaves! A toast to the sound of life that I hear, a snuffling muzzle against the grass, a dog sniffing over the ground! A resounding toast to the wildcat that lies with its throat to the ground, taking aim and preparing to spring upon a sparrow in the dark, in the dark! A toast to the merciful stillness on earth, to the stars and to the half-moon, yes, to them and to it! .

I rise and listen. No one has heard me. I sit down again.

Thanks for the solitary night, for the mountains, for the soughing of the darkness and the sea; it soughs through my heart! Thanks for my life, for my breath, for the grace of being alive tonight; for that I give thanks from my heart! Listen in the east and listen in the west, no, listen! It is the eternal God! This stillness that murmurs against my ear is the blood of all Nature seething, God weaving through the world and me. I see a shining strand of spiderweb in the light of my fire, I hear a boat being rowed in the harbor, a northern light glides upward across the sky in the north. Oh, by my immortal soul, I also give much thanks because it is I who am sitting here!

Silence. A pinecone falls dully to the ground. A pinecone fell! I think. The moon is high, the fire flickers on the half-burned brands and is about to go out. And late in the night I walk home.

The second iron night, the same stillness and the mild weather.

My soul broods. I walk mechanically over to a tree, pull my cap low over my forehead, and lean with my back against this tree, my hands clasped behind my neck. I stare and think; the flame from my fire dazzles my eyes, and I do not feel it. I stand in this senseless posture for quite some time and look at the fire; my legs are the first to fail and grow tired, and quite stiff-legged I sit down. Only now do I think about what I have done. Why stare at the fire for so long?

Aesop raises his head and listens; he hears footsteps, and Eva appears among the trees.

I am deeply pensive and sorrowful tonight, I say.
